description: Somos Team lo tre golpe. Nuestro objetivo es el desafío de Juego de diseño de misiones espaciales, combinando interactividad web, buen diseño gráfico y lógica de programación para crear una experiencia inmersiva. ¡A darle con todo!
summary:
ORBITAL COMMAND is a 3D educational space exploration video game that transforms the design and execution of space missions into an interactive experience. Players select a campaign, configure their spacecraft, and make engineering decisions that affect mass, budget, power, scientific capacity, storage, and communications.

During the mission, players plan trajectories, navigate using manual controls or automated routes, and manage resources such as fuel, power, and structural integrity. On compatible destinations, they can select landing zones, deploy a rover, explore surfaces, scan sectors, and collect samples. Afterward, they return to the station to recharge, analyze the results, and transmit a scientific report.

The game incorporates simplified orbital and planetary models for educational purposes, along with a standalone observatory that presents information from NASA and JPL with their respective sources. In this way, ORBITAL COMMAND connects engineering, navigation, and scientific exploration, allowing players to experience how decisions and resources shape the outcome of a mission.
details:
ORBITAL COMMAND: The Last Horizon is a web-based educational simulator where players design and run a complete space mission. They choose the spacecraft, instrument, power source, antenna, thermal protection and launcher; the system validates mass, budget, power and capacity, so every choice changes consumption, data and the journey. They then control the transit (simulated days, with speed ×1 to ×1000, and mandatory decisions on the way), explore destinations, carry out scientific operations and transmit a report. The campaign has 12 progressive chapters, starting on Earth and unlocking the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Europa, Saturn, Titan, Uranus, Neptune and the Sun. There are two research modes. In orbital/remote research, players use a 3D laboratory, sensors and three observation sectors. In surface exploration (Moon, Mars, Mercury and Titan), they land, drive a rover, scan three beacon locations, analyze three samples, return to the station and transmit with an educational signal delay. Telemetry tracks fuel, power, integrity, data and communication. The output is a local report with observations, samples, decisions, readings, educational references and exportable photographs. An optional commander guide offers voice, subtitles and history. An optional cooperative room supports up to four explorers with 3D avatars, chat and a shared mission through Supabase.

Benefits and expected impact: The project turns space concepts into decisions backed by evidence: gravity (~1/r²), Kepler’s T² ∝ a³, inertia and light-speed communication delay. Our context is the Dominican Republic, where PISA 2025 shows 26% of 15-year-olds at Level 2 or above in science and 9% in mathematics (OECD averages: 74% and 65%). External evidence supports the general approach: a meta-analysis of 43 studies (Putica & Stanišić, 2026) found a mean positive effect of g = 0.551 for virtual labs on conceptual science knowledge, although heterogeneity is high (I² ≈ 88%). We present this as context, not as a measured result of our simulator. We expect it to strengthen systems thinking, scientific reasoning and collaboration.

Tools and technology: React, TypeScript, Vite and Three.js for the 3D website; Supabase Auth/Realtime for accounts, teams and presence; unit tests and browser regression tests; hosting on GitHub Pages. No special hardware is needed, since it runs in a web browser. NASA/JPL resources include Blue Marble (NASA/GSFC), planetary mosaics (JPL/Caltech/USGS), mission references (Apollo, Mars 2020, Galileo, Cassini) and NASA’s Deep Space Network, all credited in the repository.

Creativity: Instead of separating design, flight, exploration and science communication, ORBITAL COMMAND joins them in one loop: Design → Explore → Analyze → Transmit. Players must justify their design, manage limited resources and communicate results, following a full chain of evidence, as a real mission does.

Factors we considered: (1) Scientific honesty: orbits, windows, distances, speeds and results are approximate/synthetic. It is not a real ephemeris, and it does not use live NASA data feeds. (2) Attribution: all NASA/JPL assets and references are credited. (3) Pedagogical limits: we do not claim a measured learning effect. (4) Accessibility: optional voice and subtitles. (5) Technical scope: the cooperative mode synchronizes presence, movement, chat and the host’s mission; flight physics and progress remain local, and it requires validating Supabase Auth, Realtime and RLS permissions before public release.

Team: Susan Castillo, Wady Cruz and Johan Torres (development), Israel J. Melo R. and Emil Castillo (research and presentation), Gabriela and Johan Torres (audiovisual communication).
